short: The first dynasty of Chinese tradition, known from later texts rather than its own records.
full:
Chinese historical tradition, set down most influentially by Sima Qian around 100 BCE, begins the dynastic sequence with the Xia, founded by Yu the Great after he tamed the floods and passed the throne to his son. No writing survives from the period itself, and no excavated inscription names the Xia, so its historicity remains genuinely disputed. The dates given here, c. 2070 to c. 1600 BCE, are those proposed by the state-funded Xia-Shang-Zhou Chronology Project in 2000 and are approximate.

What does exist is archaeology. The Erlitou culture of the Yellow River valley in Henan, flourishing roughly 1900 to 1500 BCE, built palace platforms, cast bronze ritual vessels and worked turquoise on a scale beyond any neighbouring settlement. Chinese archaeologists generally identify Erlitou with the Xia; many outside China treat the identification as unproven and read the Xia as a later dynasty's account of its own prehistory. Either way the sequence mattered: every subsequent dynasty justified itself as the latest link in a chain that began with Yu.
